title: CALLING OUT FALSE TEACHING ISN’T AUTOMATICALLY SLANDER
paragraphs:
CALLING OUT FALSE TEACHING ISN’T AUTOMATICALLY SLANDER
Sometimes Silence Looks Like Love—Until Someone You Love Swallows the Lie
There is a sentence Christians are increasingly afraid to say.
“That teaching is false.”
Not, “I hate that preacher.”
Not, “Destroy that ministry.”
Not, “Everyone who listens to them is stupid.”
Simply...
“That teaching is not faithful to Scripture.”
And almost immediately, somebody reaches for a frightening word.
Slander.
“Stop attacking people.”
“Touch not the Lord’s anointed.”
“Why are you judging?”
“Why can’t Christians just love each other?”
And because sincere believers do not want to sin with their mouths, many retreat into silence.
But there is a question we desperately need to ask before silence becomes our definition of love:
What if refusing to identify spiritual poison allows someone you love to keep drinking it?
That question matters because the Bible condemns slander—and the same Bible commands Christians to confront destructive teaching.
Both truths must remain standing.
If we erase the first, discernment can become cruelty.
If we erase the second, kindness can become cowardice.
And somewhere between those two cliffs stands Jesus Christ, who was infinitely full of grace and infinitely committed to truth.
This is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because calling something “slander” does not automatically make it slander.
And calling something “discernment” does not automatically make it righteous.
God cares about the truth you speak.
He also cares about why you speak it, how you speak it, whether you have represented someone accurately, and what you secretly hope happens to them after you speak.
That last one hurts.
Because sometimes the doctrine really is wrong...
but our heart is wrong too.
The New Testament gives us language for both dangers. James warns believers:
Μὴ καταλαλεῖτε ἀλλήλων, ἀδελφοί.
Mē katalaleite allēlōn, adelphoi.
“Do not speak against one another, brothers.”
That opening command in James 4:11 uses καταλαλεῖτε, from katalaleō—language associated with speaking against or speaking evil of another.
Scripture does not give Christians permission to turn theological disagreement into character assassination.
We do not get to invent motives.
We do not get to edit clips dishonestly.
We do not get to repeat accusations we have never verified.
We do not get to exaggerate someone’s words because the exaggerated version is easier to destroy.
We do not get to enjoy another Christian's humiliation and then baptize that enjoyment with the word “discernment.”

And there is another sobering Greek word worth knowing: διαβάλλω — diaballō, a word associated with accusing, defaming, or slandering. Its related noun διάβολος — diabolos can mean “slanderer” or “false accuser” and is famously used as a designation for the devil.
Think about that.
A Christian defending truth must never begin imitating the character of the Accuser in order to defend the God of truth.
You can win the argument and wound the body.
You can expose theological error while secretly feeding pride.
You can quote the correct verse with the wrong spirit.
You can be factually accurate and still weaponize facts maliciously.
That is why biblical discernment requires more than discovering who is wrong.
It requires examining yourself.
Before you press “post,” ask yourself something painful:
If this person publicly repented tomorrow, would I rejoice...
or would I be disappointed because I lost my enemy?
If that question makes your stomach tighten, stay there for a moment.
Jesus may be exposing something deeper than somebody else's doctrine.
But now we must face the other side.
Because Scripture's prohibition against sinful speech cannot honestly be interpreted as a prohibition against identifying false teaching.
Paul told Titus that an overseer must hold firmly to the trustworthy message so that he can both encourage others with sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it (Titus 1:9).
That is not slander.
That is pastoral responsibility.
Paul warned Timothy about people who taught different doctrine and instructed him to confront the problem (1 Timothy 1:3–7).
That is not slander.
Paul warned the Galatians about anyone preaching a gospel contrary to the one they had received (Galatians 1:6–9).
That is not slander.
Jude urged believers to “contend for the faith” entrusted to God's people (Jude 3).
That is not slander.
John warned believers not to believe every spirit but to test the spirits because false prophets had gone out into the world (1 John 4:1).
That is not slander.
And Jesus Himself warned:
“Beware of false prophets.” (Matthew 7:15)
Notice something painfully obvious.
You cannot beware of false prophets while simultaneously believing it is sinful even to recognize that false prophets exist.
Discernment requires distinctions.
Truth necessarily distinguishes truth from error.
The issue, then, is not simply, “Did you call something false?”
The deeper questions are:
Was it actually false?
Did Scripture establish that conclusion?
Did you represent the teaching accurately?
Were you correcting doctrine or assassinating character?
Were you protecting people or building an audience through outrage?
Were you grieving over deception...
or enjoying destruction?
Those questions separate biblical discernment from religious blood sport.
And Scripture gives us an astonishing example.
Peter.
Yes...
Peter.
The apostle.
The eyewitness.
The man who confessed Jesus as the Christ.
The man Jesus restored after his devastating denial.
Peter behaved in a way that compromised the truth of the Gospel.
And Paul did not shrug.
He did not say, “Peter has a huge ministry, so we should stay quiet.”
He did not say, “Who am I to judge?”
He did not hide behind a distorted version of unity.
Paul writes in Galatians 2:11:
Ὅτε δὲ ἦλθεν Κηφᾶς εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν, κατὰ πρόσωπον αὐτῷ ἀντέστην...
Hote de ēlthen Kēphas eis Antiocheian, kata prosōpon autō antestēn...
“But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face...”
To his face.
That matters.
Paul was not spreading anonymous rumors in the shadows.
He confronted a real, observable problem because Gospel truth was at stake.
And here is the beautiful part that modern outrage culture often forgets:
Peter was not Paul's disposable enemy.
Peter was his brother.
Correction was not cancellation.
Confrontation was not a declaration that grace had run out.
Peter's failure did not become the final chapter of Peter's story.
And maybe that is exactly what Christian discernment desperately needs to recover.
We expose error because we believe Jesus can still redeem people trapped in it.
Read that again.
The goal is not merely to prove someone wrong.
The goal is truth...
repentance...
restoration...
protection of Christ's sheep...
and ultimately the glory of Jesus Christ.
There is an enormous difference between saying:
“This person taught X. Scripture teaches Y. Here is the context and evidence, and here is why the distinction matters.”
and saying:
“This person is obviously a wicked fraud who never loved God and is probably doing everything for money.”
The first may be legitimate biblical criticism.
The second may involve claims about motives and hearts that you cannot possibly know.
You are not omniscient.
Neither am I.
Only God sees the heart perfectly.
That should make every discernment ministry tremble.
Because the moment exposing error becomes entertainment, something sacred has been corrupted.
Real people are involved.
Real families.
Real congregations.
Real souls.
Real wounds.
Real eternities.
This is not Christian celebrity gossip with Bible verses sprinkled over it.
Doctrine matters because people matter.

Paul told Timothy that a servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome but kind, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, and correcting opponents with gentleness, because God may grant them repentance leading to knowledge of the truth (2 Timothy 2:24–26).
There it is.
The heartbeat.
Repentance.
Not humiliation.
Not clicks.
Not “I destroyed him.”
Repentance.
The Christian does not expose darkness because he enjoys watching people burn.
He shines light because he desperately wants people to come home.
And suddenly this article is no longer about that preacher.
It is about us.
About me.
About you.
Because falsehood does not only live behind pulpits.
Sometimes it lives quietly inside our hearts.
“I can keep this sin hidden.”
“God understands, so repentance isn't necessary.”
“I am too dirty for Jesus to forgive.”
“If God loved me, I wouldn't suffer.”
“I can follow Christ without surrendering this part of my life.”
“My good works will make God accept me.”
“I don't really need Scripture; I know what feels right.”
Those are teachings too.
Some came from pulpits.
Some came from culture.
Some came from trauma.
Some came from pride.
Some came from shame.
Some were whispered so many times inside your own head that they began sounding like your voice.
And perhaps the false teacher you most urgently need to confront tonight is the voice inside you telling you something Jesus never said.
Maybe it keeps saying:
“You're too far gone.”
Look at the cross.
That is false teaching.
Maybe it says:
“Your scandal is stronger than His grace.”
Look at the empty tomb.
False.
Maybe it says:
“If people knew what you did, Jesus wouldn't want you.”
Look at Peter.
Look at the thief beside Christ.
Look at Paul.
Look at sinners eating at Jesus' table.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The Gospel says your sin was so serious that Christ died—and His grace is so magnificent that His blood can cleanse the repentant sinner.
Christianity is not God pretending scandal never happened.
It is God doing something human beings could never do with scandal.
Redeeming it.
This is why our message remains:
Not scandal to self-righteousness.
Not scandal to internet execution.
Not scandal to permanent exile.
Scandal...
to repentance...
to the cross...
to forgiveness...
to restoration...
to transformation...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And this is precisely why false teaching matters.
False doctrine eventually gives you a false picture of Christ.
A false picture of sin.
A false picture of grace.
A false picture of salvation.
A false picture of holiness.
A false picture of God.
So yes—when Scripture requires it, Christians must lovingly identify dangerous teaching.
But we must do it with trembling hands.
Tell the truth.
Show the evidence.
Open the Bible.
Represent people fairly.
Distinguish essential Gospel truth from secondary disagreements.
Never fabricate.
Never manipulate.
Never weaponize private pain.
Never pretend to know someone's hidden motives.
Never confuse disagreement with heresy.
Never confuse cruelty with courage.
Never confuse cowardice with love.
And always remember that the person you are correcting is a human being for whom repentance and mercy remain things we should desire.
Because maybe tomorrow...
you will be the one who needs correction.
That sentence changes everything.
Imagine discovering that something you confidently believed for fifteen years was wrong.
Would you want someone to mock you?
Would you want thousands celebrating your embarrassment?
Would you want your worst sentence preserved forever as if Jesus could never transform you?
Or would you want a brother or sister courageous enough to tell you the truth...
and gracious enough to leave the door open for repentance?
That is Christian correction.
Truth without love becomes a hammer.
Love without truth becomes abandonment.
But truth spoken in love can become an instrument in the hands of the Great Physician.

And if this exposed something uncomfortable in you—maybe your fear of speaking when truth matters, or perhaps the secret pleasure you have felt watching someone else fall—don't run from that conviction.
Run to Christ.
Someone reading may desperately need proof that correction does not have to end in condemnation.
And if somebody came to your mind while reading this, don't immediately send it as a weapon.
Pray first.
Then, if sharing it would genuinely serve them, send it as an invitation toward truth.

Supporting Gospel ministry should never be presented as a biblical requirement for glorifying God—Scripture does not give us permission to make that claim. But voluntary generosity, sharing sound teaching, and helping worthwhile Gospel work reach others can certainly be sincere expressions of stewardship and love for Christ.
Because we do not need more people addicted to outrage.
We need disciples who love Jesus enough to defend truth...
and love people enough to defend it without becoming cruel.
We need Christians courageous enough to say, “That teaching is false,” when Scripture clearly demands it...
humble enough to say, “I was wrong,” when Scripture corrects them...
and broken enough to say, “Jesus, have mercy on me,” when the light exposes something darker inside their own hearts.
Calling out false teaching isn't automatically slander.
But calling out false teaching does not automatically make us righteous either.
The cross leaves no room for cowardice.
And it leaves no room for pride.
At Calvary, Truth Himself was crucified for liars, slanderers, hypocrites, cowards, false accusers, religious sinners, rebellious sinners...
people like us.
And the risen Christ still transforms them.
So contend for the faith.
Guard the sheep.
Test what you hear.
Open your Bible.
Correct error.
Reject slander.
Refuse cruelty.
Welcome repentance.
Extend grace.
And never forget the person standing on the other side of your correction may yet become another breathtaking testimony that Jesus was not finished writing.
Because when Jesus holds the pen, even the chapter called “I Was Wrong” can become the beginning of somebody's restoration.
